bp: A social-media rumor leaves traces before anyone knows where it began. Some accounts have repeated it, some have not, and the platform may only see a partial snapshot of the spread. The practical question is: which earlier account or region of accounts most likely started the outbreak? That matters because moderation teams cannot slow a rumor, warn affected users, or apply sanctions efficiently if they only know the later visible spread. This paper serves that urgent traceback problem on a social graph, where accounts are points and social ties are paths along which information can travel. The task is source localization: infer the origin nodes from incomplete infection observations. LAPS focuses on making that inference usable when real misinformation cascades are scarce and time is limited. Its aim is not simply to build a larger graph model, but to reuse a trained source-region detector and adapt it cheaply to a new few-shot outbreak.
wh: The hard part is that a rumor's visible footprint is not a clean arrow pointing backward to the first account. Many different starting accounts can produce similar infected regions after several sharing steps, especially when observations are partial. A late snapshot may show a cluster of infected users, but the true source could be central, peripheral, hidden, or simply unobserved. Existing deep-learning source-localization methods try to represent each node with many extra cascade features, but the abstract says that makes the model grow explosively in parameters. The second tension is evidence scarcity: real misinformation outbreaks with trusted source labels are rare, so repeated simulations from fixed seeds can teach the model habits that do not match true few-shot outbreaks. The third tension is speed. If each new task requires full retraining or fresh cascade simulation, the method is too slow for real-time moderation, where the useful answer is needed while the rumor is still spreading.
naive: A smart beginner might look at the infected accounts and choose the most central infected node, or the account closest to all other infected nodes. That can fail because the observed infected set is incomplete and later spread can make downstream accounts look more central than the origin. Another beginner might simulate many possible rumor cascades from every candidate source and pick the simulation that best matches the snapshot. That is more principled, but it is expensive, depends on guessed diffusion behavior, and must be repeated for each new case. A deep model trained from scratch for each outbreak has the same practical problem: it may learn useful patterns, but the retraining cost and lack of real labels make it unsuitable for few-shot deployment.
ap: The core idea is to separate general source-finding knowledge from the small amount of adaptation needed for a new outbreak. LAPS first learns a reusable graph-level classifier that points to likely source regions rather than memorizing a complete cascade for every possible source. It trains this classifier on adaptive subgraphs, meaning local pieces of the social network chosen around the evidence rather than the whole graph at once. The training data uses source-prior diffusion information, so the model sees examples shaped by where sources are plausible. Then, instead of retraining the full model when a new few-shot source-localization task arrives, LAPS adds a privilege-allocation prompt module. In plain terms, the prompt is a small adjustable control layer that decides which learned signals deserve more influence for this task. The abstract emphasizes that this update touches less than one percent of the parameters, keeping adaptation lightweight.
mech: The mechanism starts with a social graph and partial infection observations. The graph gives the possible roads of spread: accounts are nodes, links are social connections or interaction paths, and infected observations mark accounts known to have received or repeated the rumor. First, LAPS forms adaptive subgraphs. Instead of feeding the entire network into an oversized model, it selects smaller regions where the source could plausibly sit, using the observed infection pattern and the graph around it. Second, before the target outbreak, it pre-trains a graph-level source region classifier. This classifier does not need to name a final exact source immediately; it learns to read a subgraph and score whether the source is likely to belong to that region. The abstract says this pre-training uses source-prior diffusion data, so the examples encode a bias toward plausible origin behavior. Third, for a new few-shot task, LAPS keeps almost all learned parameters fixed. It introduces a privilege-allocation prompt module, a small set of adjustable values that changes how much authority different learned signals receive. Fourth, only that small module is updated from the scarce new examples. The output is a source-localization decision: likely origin nodes or source regions inferred from the partial infected snapshot without full retraining or repeated cascade simulation.
math: The main mathematical object is a graph: a set of points connected by lines, where the lines describe possible routes for rumor movement. Source localization is an inverse problem. Forward spread asks, "If this account started the rumor, what infected pattern might appear later?" The inverse problem asks the harder backward question: "Given this observed pattern, what starting point could have produced it?" Because several starts can explain similar observations, the model must score candidates rather than read off a single obvious answer. Classification supplies that scoring language. A subgraph is treated as an object with a label such as likely source region or not likely source region, and training adjusts the model so its scores agree with known or simulated examples. Pre-training is reuse of repeated experience: learn broad graph-spread patterns once, then carry them into new tasks. The prompt module is parameter-efficient adaptation. Instead of changing every internal knob, it changes a tiny control surface that reallocates influence among already learned signals. The tradeoff is flexibility versus cost: full retraining can adapt more freely but is slow and label-hungry; a small prompt adapts quickly but can only steer what the pre-trained model has already learned.
dots: This paper sits in the graph source-localization thread, alongside repo evidence for another paper on continuous-time propagation via spectral ODE modeling, which also treats source finding as a backward problem from observed spread. LAPS takes a different branch: it emphasizes few-shot adaptation and deployment cost rather than solving a continuous-time propagation equation. It also connects to recurring ranking ideas because the system must score candidate regions or nodes under uncertainty and choose the most plausible origin. It connects to efficiency and scalability papers because the scarce resource is not only accuracy but also parameter count, retraining time, and repeated simulation cost. Finally, it belongs near misinformation and social-network influence work: the real object is harmful information moving through people and links, and the scientific pressure is to reason from incomplete traces before the event is over.
ww: LAPS should improve over the naive approaches because it attacks the three bottlenecks separately. Adaptive subgraphs reduce the amount of network structure the model must process, so the representation does not have to carry every possible auxiliary cascade feature for the whole graph. Pre-training a graph-level source-region classifier gives the model a stock of reusable experience about how source regions tend to look when diffusion leaves partial traces. That is better than relying only on the few labels available in a real outbreak. The privilege-allocation prompt then makes the reusable model task-sensitive without paying the cost of changing the whole model. Intuitively, the pre-trained classifier supplies the general memory, while the prompt changes which parts of that memory are trusted for the new case. This fits few-shot localization because the new evidence is too small to rebuild the full detector, yet it may still be enough to adjust the relative importance of source-prior signals, local graph shape, and infection observations.
po: The payoff is a source-localization method aimed at real-time misinformation response. According to the abstract, LAPS reduces parameter explosion, addresses data scarcity through pre-training on adaptive subgraphs with source-prior diffusion data, and adapts to few-shot tasks by updating less than one percent of all parameters. The reported experiments cover five real-world networks and show effectiveness and efficiency for few-shot source localization. In practical terms, the system promises faster adaptation to a new rumor outbreak without running full retraining or repeated cascade simulation every time moderation teams need a source estimate.
limits: The approach assumes the graph links are meaningful routes for rumor spread; if important sharing happens outside the observed network, source scores can be misleading. It also assumes source-prior diffusion data used in pre-training resembles the structure of real outbreaks closely enough to transfer. The prompt can only steer the fixed model's learned signals, so it may struggle when a new rumor spreads in a way absent from pre-training. The abstract does not specify how partial the observations are, how exact the localized source must be, or which failure cases remain on the five real-world networks. It also does not prove that punitive countermeasures based on inferred sources are fair or safe when labels are uncertain.
